newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Pro-Abacha parties favoured to win Nigerian poll.
newsitem.headline: Pro-Abacha parties favoured to win Nigerian poll.

text.p: Exit polls published on Sunday from Nigeria's local elections forecast victory for two parties who want to adopt military ruler General Sani Abacha as their candidate for civilan-rule presidential elections next year.
The independent Thisday and Sunday Concord newspapers both said the United Nigeria Congress Party (UNCP) and the Democratic Party of Nigeria (DPN) topped the poll among five legal parties.
The newspapers, based in the commercial capital Lagos, said their forecasts were based on a survey of voters by their reporters nationwide during Saturday's polling.
They gave no precise figures for how the parties would fare in the final tally of chairmen and councillors for 774 local authorities throughout the country.
"The indications do not depart significantly from the spread of the parties," Thisday said.
The trend would be in line with the rating of the National Electoral Commission (NECON) when it registered five political parties last September after the army lifted a ban on parties.

NECON said UNCP had the widest nationwide support, followed by DPN. Both are centrist with their roots in the predominantly Islamic north, which has produced most of Nigeria's leaders since independence in 1960.
Early returns from city halls in Lagos state published by Thisday and another independent daily, the Sunday Punch, showed UNCP won in five of seven municipalities declared.
Electoral authorities have yet to announce official results.
Many veteran politicians stayed on the sidelines because their parties were not registered by the military. They were expected to decide their affiliation after results are known.

The leadership of both the UNCP and the DPN have declared that they are prepared to pick Abacha as their candidate for a presidential election programmed for by September 1998 leading to the military's promised handover of power the following month.

Abacha's only comment so far on the growing controversy about the prospect of his following other military leaders in West Africa by seeking to legitimise his rule through the balot box is that it depends on his "constituency."
He has not explained if the constituency is the military or another group.
His supporters, however, say he is as free as anyone to contest elections once he quits the army.
The military government cited the peaceful local elections throughout the country as proof that its controversial civil rule plan was popular despite criticism in the West.
Information Minister Walter Ofonagoro said the orderly and enthusiastic voting showed that Nigerians endorsed the government's programme to transfer power to civilians in 1998.
"That's the way elections should be," Ofonagoro told reporters after watching polling in the city of Kaduna. "We want to show the world that Nigeria is the father of democracy."
Local observers and Western diplomats who followed Saturday's polling said they were surprised by the relaxed manner of the voting.
"It was quite orderly and smooth. Even the police were unobtrusive," said a Western diplomat in Lagos, Nigeria's largest city and a centre of opposition to the military.
More than 55 million people from a population of 100 million registered to vote.
Nigeria's then military rulers scrapped the 1993 poll as southern millionaire Moshood Abiola headed for victory and Abacha seized power in the confusion that followed.

Nigeria sank further into crisis after Abiola was detained in June 1994 for proclaiming himself president. Abacha's government fell foul of the international community when it hanged nine minority actvisits, including writer Ken Saro-wiwa, in November 1995 for murder.
